title: Mass on a spring

slow_motion.evidence: No narration, captions, or on-screen text indicate slow motion; animation plays as continuous real-time oscillation

subjects.description: small orange rectangular block attached to the lower end of a white coil spring

observation.what_happens: An orange block suspended from a spring oscillates vertically in front of a blue grid. It moves up and down continuously throughout the clip, starting mid-motion and never coming to rest or being caught.

calibration.note: scale from the fall itself: 5 px/s² over 1 arc = g of 9.807 m/s²

given: g = 9.807 m/s² (Earth); it set the scale, so treat g as known and fixed
reasoning: The path is a straight vertical line with s oscillating ~0-200 with ~0.33 s period and slowly falling peaks, sustained throughout. This matches a vertical mass-spring on Earth in air. Candidates go from textbook undamped SHM to linear viscous damping to cubic-spring plus quadratic-drag richness.

critique.finding: The block hangs on a spring that pulls with stiffness {omega} around length {s_star} while gravity pulls with {g} and slow air friction steals speed with {gamma}. That gentle slowing explains why each bounce gets a little smaller.
critique.headline: The spring keeps bouncing while air slowly steals energy.
critique.why_it_won: It captures the steady shrinking of the bounces with simple air friction, while the fancier model adds spring and drag tweaks that do not help.

headline: The spring keeps bouncing while air slowly steals energy.
finding: The block hangs on a spring that pulls with stiffness 20 ± 0.0011 1/s around length 118 m while gravity pulls with 9.81 m/s² and slow air friction steals speed with 1 ± 0.0022 1/s. That gentle slowing explains why each bounce gets a little smaller.

eyeball.confidence: low - estimate from 3 thumbnails, assumed 1m scale bar and grid, period and decay eyeballed
eyeball.law_in_words: Vertical spring-mass with gravity and linear viscous damping: m*s'' = m*g - k*(s - s_star) - c*s' with s positive downward from support, omega = sqrt(k/m), gamma = c/m, so s'' = g - omega^2*(s - s_star) - gamma*s'.
